title: Pictures and Sound as Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain how a photo becomes a grid of pixel numbers and a song becomes thousands of samples a second.
summary: A photo is a grid of pixels, each three numbers from 0 to 255 for red, green and blue. A song is samples: a CD measures the wave 44,100 times a second.

cards.headline: A photo is a grid. A song is a queue.
cards.body: Level 1 said your photo becomes numbers. But which numbers? And sound flows through time, so how does it turn into a list? Two tricks: cut space into tiny squares, and cut time into tiny slices.

cards.headline: Pixels: squares made of three numbers
cards.body: Zoom far enough into a digital photo and you reach pixels: small squares, each one color, laid out in a grid. Each pixel's color is a mix of red, green and blue light, and each of the three gets a number from 0, off, to 255, full brightness. That fits in one byte per color, so three bytes paint one pixel.

cards.fact: Three bytes per pixel allow 16,777,216 colors.
cards.context: Red, green and blue each have 256 settings, so the possible mixes number 256 × 256 × 256, or 16,777,216. Every shade in your photo is one pick from that list. Three small numbers, more than sixteen million possibilities.

cards.headline: Sound: measure, measure, measure
cards.body: To record sound digitally, a device measures the sound wave at points spaced evenly in time and writes each measurement down as a binary number, called a sample. A CD takes 44,100 samples every second. Why so many? To capture a sound you must sample more than twice as fast as its highest frequency, and human hearing reaches about 20 kHz. So CDs needed more than about 40,000 a second.

cards.headline: Pictures and sound: digitized
learned: A photo is a grid of pixels
Each pixel is red, green and blue, each 0 to 255
Sound is stored as samples: measurements of the wave
CDs sample 44,100 times a second, over twice the top of hearing

questions.prompt: How many times a second does a CD sample sound?

options.rationale: That is nowhere near enough; 20 kHz is the top of hearing.
That is far too slow to capture high sounds.
That is only the top of human hearing, not twice it.

questions.explanation: CDs take 44,100 samples a second, which is 44.1 kHz.

questions.prompt: Why would sampling music only 10,000 times a second lose the high notes?

options.label: Sampling must be more than twice as fast as the highest frequency
Each sample can only hold one note
options.rationale: A sample is one measurement of the wave, not a note.

options.label: Sound needs one sample per pixel
options.rationale: Pixels belong to pictures, not sound.

options.label: Slow sampling makes every sound louder
options.rationale: Sampling rate sets which frequencies survive, not loudness.

questions.explanation: To capture a frequency you must sample more than twice as fast. Hearing reaches about 20 kHz, so you need more than about 40,000 samples a second.

questions.prompt: Why does each red, green or blue value in a pixel fit exactly into one of Level 2's bytes?

options.label: It uses 8 digits of decimal
options.rationale: Pixels store binary, not decimal digits.

options.label: Each runs from 0 to 255: the 256 patterns of one byte
A byte holds exactly one whole pixel
options.rationale: A pixel needs three bytes, one per color.

questions.explanation: A byte has 256 patterns, exactly enough for the values 0 to 255.
